review:
Please, Don’t Touch Anything is one of those indie puzzle games built around an incredibly simple premise that gradually reveals surprising depth. Developed by Four Quarters and published by ForwardXP, the game places players in front of a strange control panel while a coworker briefly steps away. The only instruction given is clear: do not touch anything. Naturally, the entire experience is centered on ignoring that warning and discovering what happens when curiosity takes over. What begins as a seemingly harmless act of pressing a button quickly evolves into a complex web of puzzles, secrets, and unexpected consequences.

The game's greatest achievement lies in how much content it extracts from a single environment. Rather than sending players through multiple levels or locations, the entire adventure revolves around a mysterious console packed with hidden mechanisms. Every button, switch, compartment, and clue serves a purpose. At first, the panel appears limited, but each discovery reveals additional layers that transform the machine into an elaborate puzzle box. The sense of progression comes not from exploring new places but from gaining a deeper understanding of the environment directly in front of you.

Unlike traditional puzzle games that guide players toward one definitive solution, Please, Don’t Touch Anything thrives on experimentation. The game features numerous endings, each unlocked through different actions and puzzle solutions. Some outcomes are humorous, some are bizarre, and others feel surprisingly ominous. This variety encourages repeated playthroughs because every completed ending raises questions about what other possibilities remain hidden. The desire to uncover every secret becomes a powerful motivator, making the game difficult to put down despite its relatively simple structure.

The puzzle design is generally clever and rewarding. Many challenges require careful observation, logical deduction, and a willingness to test unusual ideas. The game rarely explains itself, trusting players to uncover patterns and connections independently. This hands-off approach creates satisfying moments when a solution finally clicks into place. The feeling of discovering a hidden sequence or unlocking a previously inaccessible part of the panel often delivers the same excitement as solving a much larger adventure game puzzle.

Visually, the title embraces a retro pixel-art style that suits its mysterious atmosphere perfectly. The detailed control panel feels both nostalgic and intimidating, with enough visual information to encourage investigation without becoming cluttered. Every section of the screen appears intentionally designed, and even small decorative elements may hide important clues. The minimalist presentation allows players to focus entirely on observation and experimentation, reinforcing the game's core design philosophy.

The audio contributes significantly to the overall experience. Its electronic soundtrack and subtle sound effects help create an atmosphere of curiosity and tension. Since much of the gameplay involves examining details and testing possibilities, the music provides an effective backdrop that enhances concentration without becoming distracting. Combined with the game's isolated setting, the sound design helps maintain a constant sense of mystery.

One of the most impressive aspects of the game is its replay value. Individual endings can often be reached in only a few minutes, but discovering every possible outcome requires persistence and creativity. The compact nature of each attempt ensures that replaying never feels tedious. Players can quickly reset, try a different approach, and uncover entirely new scenarios. This structure keeps the experience fresh and encourages experimentation long after the first successful ending has been achieved.

However, the game is not entirely free of frustration. Some puzzles rely on particularly obscure logic, and certain solutions can be difficult to reach without extensive trial and error. Players who prefer clear hints or a more structured progression may occasionally feel lost. While the challenge is part of the appeal, there are moments when the line between clever and cryptic becomes somewhat blurred. Fortunately, the game's relatively short play sessions help reduce the impact of these occasional frustrations.

What ultimately makes Please, Don’t Touch Anything memorable is its ability to transform curiosity into gameplay. The developers take a simple instruction and build an entire experience around the temptation to disobey it. Every interaction feels meaningful because it could lead to a new discovery, a hidden puzzle, or a completely unexpected ending. The game constantly rewards players for paying attention, experimenting, and thinking beyond obvious solutions.

For fans of puzzle games that prioritize discovery and exploration over straightforward progression, Please, Don’t Touch Anything remains a standout indie title. Its creative premise, strong replayability, clever puzzle structure, and distinctive atmosphere combine to create an experience that feels unique even years after its release. While some of its more obscure challenges may test a player's patience, the satisfaction of uncovering its many secrets makes the journey worthwhile.

-[b] A Short Summary [/b]  
A short but sweet puzzle game that is a bit cryptic at times, but has very satisfying solutions. Some of the puzzles include some meta elements, and there are pop culture references that you may or may not know, but there are some alternative ways to find some of the solutions if you look in the right places. 

-[b] The Gameplay [/b]
After the game's intro, you are presented with a screen of a city, a red button, and a billboard at the top left. Once you press the button, things start to unwind and you will start accessing new parts of the machine. Your goal from here is to find clues that will help you put specific inputs (solutions) into the machine. Different solutions will result in the screen showing different events that occur to the city, these being endings. There are 25 total endings, with each ending being unlocking a poster or art piece on the wall behind the machine.  Look around and experiment as much as you can if you want to find them all!

-[b] The Music [/b]
The soundtrack of P,DTA features a retro aesthetic that combines some aspects of old NES/Gameboy music with vaporwave aspects, making for some very ambient and nostalgic sounding tracks. Some tracks like "Screen OFF" and "Robot New" are very nostalgic and liminal, all the while being simplistic and not too invasive to the game's overall atmosphere. It's very good, I would recommend buying the soundtrack if you like the OST and want to support Four Quarters. 

-[b] 100% Completion [/b]
There are not a lot of achievements for this game, only 15 total. This makes going for that nice blue badge pretty relaxing compared to other games with longer completion times. The hardest Achievement, [i]Perfectionist,[/i] requires you to do all of the endings without pressing any of the buttons more than you need to. You are allowed to do the endings in any order besides the 25th ending - ( Don't read this if you don't want this ending spoiled [spoiler] This ending being the final ending where the machine becomes an ordinary coffee machine [/spoiler] ). This achievement sounds way worse than it is, as the devs have actually made some of the endings more forgiving so you don't mess up and accidentally click or fail an ending after a long attempt. [u]Note: I would STRONGLY recommend you play through the game once without a guide or walkthrough so you don't ruin the magic that this game has to offer you. Although, I won't blame you if you use a guide for the Perfectionist achievement afterwards[/u]


-[b] My Personal Opinion [/b]
If I had to compare PDTA to other games I have played, I would say it's kind off like FEZ, but smaller in scale and not as cryptic or meta. I didn't find myself bashing my head against a wall for hours trying to find the solution to a puzzle or ending like I did with FEZ. I strongly recommend you give this game a try, even if you have seen playthroughs of it 10-11 years ago like I did. For me, It's one of the best puzzle indie games ever made.

[h1]Please, Don't Touch Anything.[/h1]

I can see why people love this game. There is clearly a lot of affection and craft in the dense little control panel, the strange endings, the secrets, and the commitment to making a tiny interface unfold into something much bigger than it first appears. However, it's not a game for me, despite my enjoying puzzle games in general. Too much pixel hunting, the puzzle solutions are tedious and arbitrary, the font is hard to read, it is not possible to turn off the music while keeping sound effects, the fullscreen kept misaligning if I switched focus. Just... not enjoyable. I switched off when I got the "Button Maniac" accomplishment: press over 1000 buttons.

[h2]The game[/h2]

The interface is a control panel with a display screen and various hidden compartments or fold-outs that are revealed when the right button combination is pressed, that each hold their own buttons. Pressing the right sequence of buttons leads to one of a number of endings which are animated on the screen, like a mushroom cloud or a meteor or a giant robot, and then the interface resets. Each ending collects a sticker, and presumably the idea is to find them all.

[h2]My experience[/h2]

I personally did not feel a sense of accomplishment when finding an ending, just a sense of exhaustion after a tedious flurry of pressing different buttons, trying out different arbitrary ideas. The giant robot "Kill All Humans" ending comes [spoiler]after you open a binary panel and notice that there is a binary sequence represented on the instruction panel and press that sequence[/spoiler]. Why that ending at that moment? [i]*Shrug*[/i] The meteor ending also comes after an arbitrary set of trying out different ideas. In that case it is [spoiler]after managing to open a 3-tone keyboard, and noticing that the background music has a melody, and inputting that melody[/spoiler]. Why then? Why not!?

I am currently playing [i]Epigraph[/i], and although I have not solved it yet, I am enjoying it. That game is also obscure and demanding, but the process feels more like gradually understanding a system. [i]Please, Don’t Touch Anything[/i] felt to me more like hunting for hidden affordances and trying input sequences until something happened. That can be satisfying if you enjoy this kind of compact, secret-filled puzzle box. For me, it became tiring rather than rewarding.

Not recommended, but not because it is badly made. It is not lazy or careless. It is just built around a kind of puzzling that does not work well for me. It is a lovingly made game whose particular kind of obscurity, repetition, and pixel hunting I did not enjoy.

Please, Don’t Touch Anything starts with the simplest instruction ever given in a video game:
“Don’t touch anything.”

Naturally, this is the fastest way to guarantee that every player immediately starts touching everything.

You’re left alone in a room with a mysterious red button and a control panel that looks like it was designed by someone who hates humanity. Your coworker steps away for “a minute,” which in video game time means long enough for you to accidentally destroy the universe.

Press the button once? Something weird happens.
Press it twice? Something worse happens.
Start flipping switches and entering random codes? Congratulations, you just triggered an ending where reality itself files a complaint.

The whole game is basically curiosity vs. consequences. Every tiny interaction can lead to a completely different outcome, and many of those outcomes involve things going very wrong for the city outside the window.

The puzzles are clever, cryptic, and occasionally make you feel like you’re decoding messages from a conspiracy theorist’s notebook. When you finally figure one out, you feel like a genius… until the ending reveals you’ve just caused another catastrophe.

The retro pixel-art style fits perfectly, making the whole experience feel like you discovered a very dangerous machine from the 1980s that absolutely should not be left unattended.

9/10 Curiosity didn’t just kill the cat. It destroyed the city.
